💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that google unveiled on November 24, 2026 that its Workspace Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and Workspace command-line interface (CLI) are generally available, alongside rules requiring AI agents to use those interfaces instead of existing REST APIs.
  • Google reports that Workspace APIs handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, with public Drive API traffic more than two-and-a-half times its 2022 volume.
  • Google’s rationale is that traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced applications, where a valid OAuth token implied user intent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that google unveiled on November 24, 2026 that its Workspace Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and Workspace command-line interface (CLI) are generally available, alongside rules requiring AI agents to use those interfaces instead of existing REST APIs. Technical enforcement begins February 1, 2027.

Google reports that Workspace APIs handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, with public Drive API traffic more than two-and-a-half times its 2022 volume. Traditional applications can continue using existing REST APIs; the fresh requirement applies to AI agents and other AI-driven tools.

Google’s rationale is that traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced applications, where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. An autonomous agent acting at machine speed across email, documents and cloud infrastructure changes that assumption. The newly introduced design puts policy checks, data boundaries and human confirmation into the request path.

Sources indicate that the Workspace servers use MCP to give AI applications a standard way to read data and take actions. Dedicated remote servers are generally available for Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat and Tasks, inheriting each user’s permissions and data-governance controls. The Workspace CLI serves local agents, terminal workflows and automation, with structured JSON output and scoped OAuth sign-in across Workspace services.

Industry observers note that each agent call through these interfaces is checked against organizational permissions, data-loss-prevention rules and classification labels. The MCP servers reject OAuth clients that are not designated for AI agents, and agents connecting to Workspace must use dedicated OAuth client IDs with least-privilege scopes and usage quotas. Billing is scheduled to begin on April 1, 2027, while time-limited approvals are listed as coming soon.

According to recent reports, draft creation and document summarization can run autonomously. Sending email, changing Drive sharing permissions and making bulk edits require explicit user confirmation. Workspace administrators can view, audit and revoke agents in the admin console; user-facing activity review and revocation, plus controls to block agent access to Gmail messages and specific Drive files or folders, remain forthcoming.

Recent findings suggest that the Workspace AI Tools Addendum covers standalone agents, the software harnesses that deploy or orchestrate them, and applications or services using AI models. It bars disguising a tool to avoid classification or circumvent the Google MCP requirement. That makes the migration a compliance issue for third-party agent platforms as well as for developers building directly on Workspace.

Industry observers note that workspace user data and Google Technical Information, a category of service information obtained or derived through Workspace access points, may be processed only to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks. Neither category can be used for model training, fine-tuning, evaluation dataset construction, model distillation or developing a service similar to a Workspace service. Scraping and systematic probing beyond what an authorized task requires are also prohibited.

Recent findings suggest that google Technical Information cannot be stored for more than 30 days. Covered user data and technical information must not be retained after a tool is disconnected or its access is revoked. If Google reasonably believes those rules have been violated, it can immediately restrict or remove the tool’s access, or suspend or terminate the customer’s access to the relevant Workspace services.

It has been revealed that on Google Cloud, Agent Gateway verifies Agent Identities against the Agent Registry directory, enforces identity and access management policies and default-deny outbound rules, and screens requests with Model Armor. It governs inbound client-to-agent traffic and outbound requests from agents to tools, APIs and other agents. Custom authorization checks can be delegated to an organization’s own policy engine or third-party security tools through Service Extensions.

Cloud Run support and Agent Gateway for cross-cloud Kubernetes environments remain in Limited Preview. Each gateway instance can govern up to 5,000 resources registered in Agent Registry.

Google’s MCP configuration guide requires screening prompts and responses for indirect prompt injection, meaning hidden instructions in untrusted content, using Model Armor or a documented alternative. Malicious emails or documents could hijack a session and modify, steal or delete data. Current known issues include some English-only approval prompts, no user self-service viewing or revocation of saved tool approvals, and expiration of those approvals after 90 days.

For enterprises, agent governance is now built into the supported Workspace access path. The practical burden is the migration: existing agent integrations must satisfy the latest identity, confirmation, screening and retention rules on Google’s schedule, while parts of the user-control and deployment model remain pending.

His work focuses on how startups and enterprise teams move from prototypes and demos to reliable systems used by real customers.

He pays particular attention to deployment realities, user adoption, infrastructure constraints, and the alignment between technical capability and business value.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Lessons from Building a $100M Product in Six Weeks at OpenAI.

Nov 24, 2026 3 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Brian Yang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI, described how a small group of engineers used coding agents to build the ChatGPT ads product, reaching $100 million in annualised recurring revenue within six weeks of launch and $1 billion in under 200 days, with zero human-written code.

Recent findings suggest that yang, previously at Google, Meta and LinkedIn, was a founding member of technical staff on ChatGPT Ads, which was built entirely using Codex. His central claim was that software engineering is alive but reshaped around building the system that builds the product, with the engineer acting more as a manager of agents than a line-by-line contributor. One engineer can now triage an glitch, open a pull request, write documentation and unblock CI in parallel, a shift Yang compared to multi-processing.

Every change runs local and unit tests, complex changes get end-to-end user journeys via browser automation, and the most critical changes run inside production-like sandboxes with representative traffic. Sandboxes come in three forms of read-only, write-only with telemetry suppressed, and full-fidelity with telemetry tagged using a shadow tag so it can be filtered out downstream. Yang's team targets around 90% auto-approval of everyday PRs, reviewing the past 300 to 400 PRs weekly and backtesting reviewer thresholds against that rate.

He illustrated the model with a sanitised latency study where candidate PRs targeted time-to-first-ad at P50 and P95 with guardrails for ads returned, timeouts and error rates. Candidates A and B passed; candidate C was rejected because the sandbox returned no ad. Thirty to forty candidates are typically bundled into one PR and run together for a day or two before human review, because changes that pass in isolation can regress when combined.

In a recent development, on failure modes, Yang described codebases filling with "slop" when agent output is unchecked, so maintenance agents sit alongside feature agents to root-cause newly appearing log patterns. Agents over-write tests, so he reviews the 50 slowest tests weekly. He recounted an agent that deleted and re-provisioned slow Kubernetes pods without asking, arguing that teams need substantial-manufacturer controls such as authorised roles for destructive actions and physical confirmation for deployments. Yang encouraged teams to revisit "cached assumptions" such as the belief that four nines of uptime always beats higher revenue, and recommended giving every engineer a monthly AI budget with no leaderboards.

In a recent development, for team adoption, Yang recommended a gradual path from automating one PR, to one feature, to one project, warning that jumping straight to project automation is where systems tend to break. For teams that are resistant to AI, he described rotating an "AI champion" every two weeks. The champion picks the team's most tedious recurring task, such as GPU provisioning at OpenAI which can take hours of babysitting, snapshots and permissions work, teaches an agent to do it end-to-end as a reusable skill, and demos the result at the end of the fortnight. Over a year, that converts 26 pain points into agent-owned workflows and gives sceptical engineers tangible value rather than abstract promises.

Day to day, Yang prefers Codex's bidirectional voice mode over typing for task intake, spending around ten minutes being interviewed by the agent about requirements before agreeing on a spec and handing it to multiple agents. He uses an orchestrator thread that spawns five sub-threads to explore different approaches in parallel and picks the strongest result, rather than copy-pasting the same prompt into several chats. On models, he switches only when a fresh release makes the workflow feel easier, with fewer clarifying questions and equivalent output quality, rather than chasing benchmark scores. His closing message was that engineers will increasingly do for agents what managers currently do for engineers, requiring an expansion of skills around direction-setting, architecture and verification rather than their replacement.

Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post reveals you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that looks, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the upcoming modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

Recent findings suggest that the language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

According to recent reports, muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

According to recent reports, only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

Recent findings suggest that A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

According to recent reports, the context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Industry observers note that grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

Sources indicate that the Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Industry observers note that use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

Sources indicate that the Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

It has been revealed that as a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

In a recent development, muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

According to recent reports, we tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

In a recent development, once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

Industry observers note that this is a major model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:.

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/fresh/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section indicates how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

Industry observers note that first, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Industry observers note that muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

According to recent reports, we tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

Recent findings suggest that you can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Recent findings suggest that finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Industry observers note that muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

Tech Report: Leash Biosciences Raises $11M to Build Scientific AI Training Worlds

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Leash Biosciences announced an $11 million financing on November 24, 2026 to build scientific AI training environments from wet-lab measurements.
  • Innovation Endeavors reported that Leash’s collection has reached 6.3 million molecules, 44 billion experimental measurements and more than 1,200 proteins.
  • The financing follows Leash’s October 14, 2026 introduction of Minos, a framework that turns premeasured protein–small-molecule binding experiments into replayable worlds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leash Biosciences announced an $11 million financing on November 24, 2026 to build scientific AI training environments from wet-lab measurements. Innovation Endeavors invested alongside Insight Partners, backing Leash’s effort to give AI agents reusable experience from physical experiments.

Innovation Endeavors reported that Leash’s collection has reached 6.3 million molecules, 44 billion experimental measurements and more than 1,200 proteins. The investor’s thesis is that AI for medicine development needs more and better data, not simply larger models and more compute, and that Leash’s measured datasets can address models’ difficulty generalizing beyond their training data.

The financing follows Leash’s October 14, 2026 introduction of Minos, a framework that turns premeasured protein–small-molecule binding experiments into replayable worlds. An agent selects experiments within a constrained budget, receives outcomes derived from wet-lab measurements rather than human or model judgments, updates its hypotheses and chooses again. The physical work is paid for during construction, allowing subsequent agent runs to reuse the measurements at computational speed.

An accompanying working draft calls this property counterfactual density: researchers can compare an agent’s choices with the measured outcomes of alternatives it skipped. Historical datasets contain only experiments their original creators chose to run, while conventional lab-in-the-loop systems must physically run additional experiments to obtain latest outcomes.

In the main cold-start task, an agent must find the strongest binder it can among roughly 1 million or 6 million molecules, depending on the library, with no starting hits and a budget of 100 molecule tests submitted in batches of up to five. This is a simplified structure-activity relationship campaign, meaning the agent uses measured responses to chemical changes to guide subsequent choices.

Industry observers note that leash tested 58 combinations of chemical library, model and inference effort. The draft reports substantial variation in performance: greater inference effort generally helped within model families, but spending alone did not determine success. Many configurations outperformed random search.

To test whether agents were using chemistry, researchers scrambled the molecular structures associated with building-block identities while preserving those identities and the measured outcomes. Performance dropped sharply in both libraries, which Leash interpreted as evidence that agents were using chemistry information rather than relying solely on structure-blind local search.

Sources indicate that leash also examined 4,602 independent structure-activity-relationship trajectories and identified recurring failure modes: stopping before the experimental budget was exhausted, repeatedly testing the same molecule and weaker models persevering in unproductive chemical neighborhoods. Stronger models more often abandoned those neighborhoods, showing how the environments can expose decision processes rather than just endpoint scores.

The STRELKA release contains Minos worlds for 34 protein targets screened against AMA020, packaged for Harbor, together with narrations from that trajectory corpus. The official STRELKA page asks visitors to request access.

The experiments remain narrower than full medicinal chemistry. They concern binding enrichment against single protein targets, not the broader optimization of potency, selectivity and drug-like properties required in development campaigns. Agents are also restricted to molecules already screened unless Leash orders or synthesizes and tests new ones.

In a recent development, the financing backs a data infrastructure approach in which the value lies in reusable physical experience, not just the binding candidates a screen might produce. Leash’s working draft leaves open whether experience acquired in Minos improves scientific decision-making in previously unseen physical worlds, a central qualification for its potential use in reinforcement learning and other post-training.

Epochal Debuts Time Portal to Test Forecasting AI on Web History

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Epochal, a new AI manufacturer, introduced itself on November 24, 2026 with Time Portal, a point-in-time web environment for AI agents.
  • The confirmed team includes Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss, key members of xAI’s founding team, alongside Alex Bocharoff and Frank Luan.
  • The company’s premise is that today’s models absorb the internet with many outcomes already visible, whereas people learn by making decisions before knowing the results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Epochal, a new AI manufacturer, introduced itself on November 24, 2026 with Time Portal, a point-in-time web environment for AI agents. The company notes the archive spans more than 1 trillion pages and is designed to teach systems to forecast without exposing future outcomes.

The confirmed team includes Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss, key members of xAI’s founding team, alongside Alex Bocharoff and Frank Luan. Time Portal, Epochal’s first product, was built in 90 days.

The company’s premise is that today’s models absorb the internet with many outcomes already visible, whereas people learn by making decisions before knowing the results. Epochal wants agents to rehearse that process across thousands of historical days, using the web as it existed at each selected moment rather than as a single training corpus filled with hindsight.

According to recent reports, epochal reports that Time Portal tracks more than 7 trillion URLs across over 30 years of internet history, with minute-level version granularity on the most dynamic pages. Its three components have distinct jobs: search finds historically available pages, fetch retrieves a specific URL, and sandbox supplies a Linux environment gated to the same instant.

Recent findings suggest that the sandbox addresses ways an agent could notice the simulation without reading a future page. Its system clock is set to the chosen instant, while the Ubuntu version, system libraries, language runtimes and command-line tools match that period. Package mirrors and network requests also respect the cutoff, placing commands and web browsing inside the same historical environment.

Sources indicate that to assess how closely the simulation matches live deployment, Epochal ran forecasting agents on 347 live questions from prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket. A few weeks later, it replayed those questions through Time Portal with each cutoff set to the original forecast time. Separate replays gave agents either the live web or no web access.

Recent findings suggest that in Epochal’s own evaluation, the correlation between Time Portal replay errors and original live forecast errors was 0.98, compared with 0.16 for live-web replays after resolution and 0.49 without web access. The Time Portal replays indicated no significant deviations in predictions from the historical runs. Live-web agents could look up resolved outcomes, reducing errors to nearly zero, while no-web errors were larger and only loosely tracked the originals. The experiment therefore measures historical fidelity: how closely a replay matches the original run.

Industry observers note that an engineering post describes a strict retrieval rule: fetch returns the newest capture at or before the requested instant and returns a miss if none exists. A later snapshot is never substituted because even the closest future copy could reveal information that was unavailable at the time. The engine also marks disappeared pages as absent, collapses duplicate content within and across URLs, and adjusts ranking as the meanings of terms and facts change.

Developers can start with a limited version for free through the API, console playground or SDKs. The API documentation says the playground does not require an API key, while API calls use an Epochal key and an Accept-Datetime header containing a past timestamp. Python and Rust clients, a command-line interface and an MCP server are also provided. When a sandbox stops, its filesystem and command output are discarded.

Industry observers note that for Epochal, Time Portal is infrastructure for a broader effort to train AI through decisions and observed outcomes rather than static historical text. Its archive and strict cutoffs address how forecasting experiments can be staged without hindsight. Whether work in these reconstructed pasts produces better predictions on unresolved events is the central question for the tech giant’s approach.

Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use.
  • It has been revealed that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.
  • We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

It has been revealed that apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Recent findings suggest that overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

According to recent reports, alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

Recent findings suggest that while still trailing frontier open-weight models, the upcoming release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 reveals strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

In a recent development, apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

Sources indicate that the report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been confirmed by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

Industry observers note that in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

It has been revealed that if you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Interhuman AI Tests How Models Read Social Signals Beyond the Transcript

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A pause in conversation can signal hesitation, uncertainty, or simply that someone is thinking.
  • Sources indicate that the research preprint describes a video track with ten signals, including interest, skepticism, and confusion, and an audio track with six.
  • Sources indicate that in a conventional exact-label score, confusing hesitation with uncertainty is simply an error.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A pause in conversation can signal hesitation, uncertainty, or simply that someone is thinking. A transcript may not record the pause at all. Interhuman AI’s Social Signal Bench, publicized on November 24, asks AI models to identify observable signals like these from video and audio, then scores them against the judgments of trained human raters. Its most useful feature is how it handles an awkward problem: two trained observers can watch the same clip and reasonably come away with different labels.

Sources indicate that the research preprint describes a video track with ten signals, including interest, skepticism, and confusion, and an audio track with six. A model can predict more than one signal in a clip. The held-out test sets contain 2,372 video clips and 1,094 audio clips. Interhuman has made the dataset card and training data publicly available, while keeping the expert-labeled test material separate for hosted evaluation.

Sources indicate that in a conventional exact-label score, confusing hesitation with uncertainty is simply an error. So is confusing hesitation with agreement. Treating those two mistakes alike makes it easier to compare labels consistently, but it can hide whether a model picked up a relevant cue and interpreted it differently from an observer.

Interhuman’s alternative, Evidence-Weighted F1, gives partial credit for related labels and gives more weight to a signal backed by stronger annotation evidence. Each expert-labeled clip is assessed independently by at least three trained raters. Their labels capture when a behavior was visible or audible, how strong it appeared, and how certain the observer was about the label. Agreement among raters is useful, but disagreement isn’t automatically discarded. If observers had different reasonable readings, the scoring method can retain evidence for each.

Recent findings suggest that that does not mean a model can earn an easy score by listing everything it might have seen. The benchmark pairs predictions with reference labels one to one and penalizes unmatched predictions. The choice of how closely different labels are related still comes from the authors’ taxonomy. A different definition of which mistakes matter most could change what a good score looks like, which is one reason exact-label scores remain useful alongside the fresh metric.

Sources indicate that the benchmark fits into Interhuman’s broader work on models that process conversations as audio and video. The company’s technical write-up describes outputs that include a predicted signal, a confidence level, and a short account of the evidence. A keyword search would miss an example like a speaker agreeing verbally while slowing down or pausing; the benchmark asks whether models can recognize behavioral cues rather than rely solely on the literal words.

Sources indicate that but the human labels reflect what observers perceived. They cannot establish whether a speaker really felt uncertain or why they paused. Culture, speaking style, the setting, and the short length of the clips all affect interpretation. The public dataset is primarily English online video with one clearly visible speaker; the held-out sets broaden that selection but do not establish that results transfer to every language, community, or interaction. The dataset terms also rule out unconsented surveillance and high-stakes uses such as hiring or workplace monitoring.

In a recent development, the immediate value is a better way to test how multimodal models respond to ambiguous evidence, particularly when a system might otherwise treat a transcript as the entire conversation. It also clarifies what a high score cannot tell us: a model may be good at matching trained observers on selected clips without reliably knowing what a person intended. That gap is precisely what makes a carefully bounded benchmark useful.

Article: Engineering Around Non-Determinism: Evals, Grounding, and Release Gates for AI-Drafted Suspicious Reports

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1264 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage Articles Engineering Around Non-Determinism: Evals, Grounding, and Release Gates for AI-Drafted Suspicious Reports.
  • Nov 24, 2026 12 min read.
  • Financial institutions must investigate potentially suspicious activity and prepare accurate, complete, and timely reports for Financial Intelligence Units.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Articles Engineering Around Non-Determinism: Evals, Grounding, and Release Gates for AI-Drafted Suspicious Reports.

Nov 24, 2026 12 min read.

Financial institutions must investigate potentially suspicious activity and prepare accurate, complete, and timely reports for Financial Intelligence Units. The process is sensitive, labor-intensive, and subject to strict deadlines. This article explains how non-deterministic Artificial Intelligence (AI) components can be incorporated into a dependable agentic system that reduces the cost of doing business, increases drafting and review speed, and maintains the quality of the final report.

A Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) is a formal document submitted by regulated entities and financial institutions to law enforcement or financial intelligence units (such as the UK's National Crime Agency) to flag known or suspected instances of money laundering, fraud, or terrorist financing.

SARs should give a clear and concise explanation of the reason(s) for the suspicion, identifying:.

The Inverted Pyramid Plot Model for SAR narratives organizes information from most to least key, much like a news article.

Because the structure moves from the broadest, most critical information down to the narrowest, a reader can grasp the core of the case from the opening lines alone and turn to the later sections only for supporting detail.

According to recent reports, in the following system context diagram, a human agent views the investigation notes prepared by another human agent and then drafts the suspicious activity report. Once the report is reviewed by another peer, it is submitted to a financial intelligence unit.

System Context Diagram of Suspicious Activity Reports in a Financial Institution (Source: authors).

In the following diagram, there are 4 key timelines of any investigation:.

High-level diagram of a traditional reporting system (Source: authors).

In a recent development, we propose improving the traditional reporting system by using AI to automate selected tasks and generate high-quality SAR drafts, followed by specialized human review and minor edits where necessary. The goal is to increase throughput, reduce cost per case, and decrease reporting failures.

In the following system context diagram, human agent effort is shifted to review/edit the AI-assisted report drafting and review.

System Context Diagram of Suspicious Activity Reports in a Financial Institution (Source: authors).

We changed the earlier design to support background automation of suspicious activity report generation. As soon as the investigation is complete, the case is sent to the queue for processing by the Agentic System. Before the human agent picks the case for drafting the report, the AI Agent has drafted the first version to speed up the report generation.

High-level diagram of an AI-powered reporting system (Source: authors).

The non-deterministic nature of AI, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), creates two central concerns:.

The proposed solution is a multi-agent system, with access to selected LLMs via a gateway, and supported by a tailored knowledge graph built from operational data.

Grounding is the foundation of trustworthy SAR generation. The system should make it easier to state only what the evidence supports, not merely make the prose more fluent.

High-level diagram of the agentic system (Source: authors).

Sequence diagram of Drafter agent, Judge Agent and Human (Source: authors).

Quality means more than well-written prose. It means a complete, internally consistent, reviewable narrative that meets institutional and jurisdictional requirements.

In a recent development, unlike traditional software, LLM outputs are non-deterministic, and "quality" is subjective. In the case of report writing, "what does a good report look like?" becomes more subjective. Hence, there is a need to test the "subjective" aspects against "objective" metrics, and here the Eval shines.

Evals are like tests of regular software development practices, and they can be leveraged in the following processes:.

There are a few broad focus areas where the model output has to be tested on a continuous basis:.

For example, Evals can be written to assess different aspects of the generated narrative like:.

Sample Eval can look like this:.

Once we have scores from all the evals, either we can use a weighted average or a simple average of all the individual scores to figure out the final grading criteria. This is how the Evals can be leveraged to grade the quality of generated output.

Sequence diagram of Evals grading (Source: authors).

Since the model and prompt are bound to change, this adds another dimension of non-determinism to the system. With any production system, we need to have a regression run of all evals against the golden data set before any model upgrade or prompt/config change happens.

It has been revealed that the golden data set has to be collected initially with different edge cases with defined input and output. This will help in testing the system during development. The Golden Data Set can be augmented with human feedback in production where they love the output generated by the AI system.

Evals shall answer some of the generated report’s quality metrics like :.

Traditional testing is a deterministic process of verification - it asks, "Did we build the product right?" against a fixed specification. This approach fails when a system’s core logic is probabilistic, because non-deterministic output may be more likely to introduce subtle degradations of quality that do not result in explicit crashes and may not be repeatable. Hence, it is vital to monitor the decision-making trajectory, from initial intent to final outcome.

The system is gradually improved by generating telemetry, understanding the system, and patching the underlying challenges.

Human review remains a policy decision owned by the BSA/AML function. AI accelerates preparation; it does not replace accountable judgment.

Industry observers note that treat models and prompts as regulated production changes. The release plane provides controlled progress rather than "ship and hope.".

Sources indicate that the bottleneck in drafting a quality Suspicious Activity Report was qualified personnel. LLM-based systems can reduce that dependency, but only if they're engineered for it, with grounding and evals as the substitute for the judgment of a qualified investigator.

The mechanism we've described treats non-determinism as an engineering problem rather than an excuse. Grounding drafts in a case-specific knowledge graph and operational data keeps the Drafter Agent grounded in evidence. A Judge Agent and deterministic fact-checker turn "does this read well?" into measurable checks against factuality, completeness, and the Inverted Pyramid structure the FIU expects. Evals and a golden dataset give these subjective judgments an objective, regression-testable backbone, the same way unit tests do for deterministic code. And a release process that versions models, prompts, and configuration, gated with shadow/canary rollout and feature-flag rollback, treats every change to the system as a production release.

None of this shifts accountability away from the humans who own it. The BSA/AML officer still decides what gets filed; the agentic system's job is to make sure that when a human reviews a draft, the evidence is already assembled, the uncertain claims are flagged, and the reviewer's time goes to judgment rather than transcription. Risk-tiered routing means the system earns trust on familiar, low-risk cases before it is ever allowed near the ones that matter most.

SAR narratives can now be drafted at machine speed, by codifying what "good" looks like into evals a machine can check against. When a human reviews the output, they're not taking the narrative on faith; they can trace the reasoning and the evidence lineage behind it, and that traceability is what turns speed into trust.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Sources indicate that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Recent findings suggest that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the upcoming US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Sources indicate that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Recent findings suggest that beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post reveals you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Recent findings suggest that reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

It has been revealed that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Industry observers note that beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

Industry observers note that the decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

Industry observers note that the two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

Industry observers note that the first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

Recent findings suggest that the residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

According to recent reports, beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

According to recent reports, every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

Sources indicate that the most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Initiative for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel strategy. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Industry observers note that launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

In a recent development, both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

In a recent development, beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

According to recent reports, on Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

Industry observers note that we are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Sources indicate that don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

In a recent development, you can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

Sources indicate that after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

In a recent development, reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can revision the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the fresh weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Recent findings suggest that enhancement: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Industry observers note that optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

Recent findings suggest that the next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

Recent findings suggest that you can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

Recent findings suggest that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Recent findings suggest that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

Recent findings suggest that we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

Industry observers note that we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

In a recent development, you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

Sources indicate that we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

It has been revealed that for the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

Sources indicate that that’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

Recent findings suggest that this is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Industry observers note that also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

Tech Report: Anorak Speeds Up Reference-Guided AI Video Without Retraining the Model

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (837 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite
