📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A video generator asked to follow reference footage can spend a surprising share of its time revisiting details that barely change: an empty sky, a flat wall, or a stretch of road.
  • The distinction matters for anyone evaluating faster video generation.
  • It has been revealed that reference-guided generation lets a creator provide more than a prompt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A video generator asked to follow reference footage can spend a surprising share of its time revisiting details that barely change: an empty sky, a flat wall, or a stretch of road. In a release on November 24, Anorak mentioned its AI lab had developed a way to cut that repeated work. The method improved end-to-end generation speed by about 1.5 to 1.6 times on two benchmarks in the team’s research preprint, without retraining the underlying model. A separate result that exceeded twice the original speed combined the method with another optimization.

The distinction matters for anyone evaluating faster video generation. The authors measured one model, a version of MiniMax-H3 already optimized with eight denoising timesteps and 8-bit quantization. The findings suggest there was still meaningful room to reduce computation in an already streamlined system. They do not show that the method halves generation time across video models or makes them responsive enough for live interaction.

It has been revealed that reference-guided generation lets a creator provide more than a prompt. An image can supply the appearance of a character, while a rough animation can show the motion or composition a finished clip should follow. In the architecture studied by the researchers, the model represents those references as tokens and examines them alongside the tokens for the output it is generating. Reference tokens account for roughly half of that combined sequence in the configuration described in the paper. Longer sequences are expensive because full attention compares tokens with one another; the number of those comparisons grows roughly with the square of sequence length.

It has been revealed that yet not every part of a reference contributes equally. A patch of sky that barely changes from frame to frame adds less latest information than a moving subject. There is an crucial exception: a static detail can still be central to what the creator asked for. A logo on a moving car may be visually repetitive across the reference but essential to the shot.

It has been revealed that anorak calls its method PCRG, short for pruning and caching of reference tokens for video generation. It uses two signals the system already produces. The first indicates whether the compressed visual information is repetitive. The second, drawn from the part of the system that reads the visual inputs and prompt together, helps identify which pieces of the reference are relevant to the output.

According to recent reports, the method keeps processing tokens that add distinctive information. It processes repetitive but relevant tokens once, then reuses part of that computation as the clip is refined. It drops repetitive tokens that the system identifies as less relevant before those refinement passes start. Instead of asking the model to do fewer rounds of refinement, the method reduces how much reference information it has to reconsider in each round. That difference explains why it can be combined with some other speedups.

According to recent reports, the researchers reported a 1.57× end-to-end speedup on their V2V-Bench test suite and 1.49× on the public VACE-Benchmark. Their VBench quality measure declined by 0.24% and 0.17%, respectively. Combining PCRG with Veda reached 2.15× on V2V-Bench. These are author-reported results, and a small change in an aggregate score cannot rule out errors in an individual clip.

In a recent development, for Anorak, the research is part of a broader effort to make generated footage respond to players. Workflows that repeatedly adjust a reference or generate alternative takes could benefit even if the technology falls short of real-time play. How far the gains extend is an open question: a workflow with short or little reference material has less redundant input to remove, and a model that handles references differently may not see the same improvement. The next useful evidence would be a comparison across more model families and longer, more varied inputs, with timings and visual quality reported together.

Anthropic Brings Server-Supplied Skills and Background Tasks to Claude

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (928 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, anthropic announced on November 24, 2026 that Skills over MCP is in public beta in Claude and Claude Code, while Tasks and Elicitation are generally available and File Uploads will roll out soon.
  • The features are built around the open Model Context Protocol (MCP) and its extension system, allowing supporting servers to work in compatible clients beyond Claude.
  • Tool names and descriptions tell Claude what a server can do; skills add guidance on how to handle particular use cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, anthropic announced on November 24, 2026 that Skills over MCP is in public beta in Claude and Claude Code, while Tasks and Elicitation are generally available and File Uploads will roll out soon. The additions let connected servers supply workflow guidance, run lengthy jobs, request user input and, once File Uploads arrives, exchange files with Claude.

The features are built around the open Model Context Protocol (MCP) and its extension system, allowing supporting servers to work in compatible clients beyond Claude. Anthropic reports more than 700 million monthly MCP SDK downloads and over 10,000 MCP connectors for Claude, describing the ecosystem it is asking to implement the fresh server capabilities.

Tool names and descriptions tell Claude what a server can do; skills add guidance on how to handle particular use cases. A server can publish best practices, step-by-step workflows or playbooks tailored to a user’s account or organization alongside its tools. Claude retrieves a skill only when needed, and updates arrive with the server, so users do not install anything separately.

Industry observers note that the Skills extension documentation defines a skill as a directory containing a SKILL.md file and optional supporting files, with discovery and retrieval handled through MCP’s existing Resources primitive. Hosts may not fetch files ahead of need. Before use, they must verify each file’s byte size and SHA-256 digest and compare the instruction file’s frontmatter with the approved manifest; changed files require fresh approval. SDK and host support across clients is still being implemented.

It has been revealed that the beta is on by default for Pro, Max and Ultra looks, available to Team plans after an administrator enables it, and listed as coming soon to Enterprise. Anthropic’s examples include Shopify for designing and updating online stores, HubSpot for customer onboarding and Atlassian for organization-specific analysis. A forthcoming Carta skill is intended to draft and glitch equity from an uploaded document.

Tasks and Elicitation are available to Pro, Max and Ultra plans in Claude and Claude Code and are rolling out to Team and Enterprise organizations. Tasks lets a server run a time-consuming operation or a full agent loop in the background while Claude continues other work and retrieves the result later. ZoomInfo uses it for deeper account and contact research that previously required several prompts.

It has been revealed that the Tasks documentation claims the server returns a durable task handle instead of blocking the connection. Clients can poll for progress and resume with the same task ID after a disconnect or restart. States cover working, input required, completion, failure and cancellation, and a task can request input before proceeding. Cancellation is cooperative, so the server acknowledges the request without being obligated to stop the underlying work.

Industry observers note that elicitation lets a server pause for user input through a form or link before continuing. Supabase uses it to confirm paid-project costs and destructive SQL, Railway to ask before potentially destructive changes, and GitHub to request a repository name before deletion. The Elicitation specification separates structured form input from URL-based interactions and bars servers from using forms to request passwords, API keys, access tokens or payment credentials. Clients must identify the requesting server and provide decline and cancel options.

Anthropic prepares File Uploads for Claude and Claude Code on Pro, Max, Ultra and eligible Team and Enterprise plans. It will allow PDFs, spreadsheets and images to pass to MCP servers without going through the model’s context window.

The File Uploads repository makes its earlier-stage status explicit: the extension is experimental, is not part of the MCP specification and has not been proposed for inclusion, so breaking changes are expected. Its design keeps file bytes out of model context and JSON-RPC messages. A server marks file arguments, the client uploads missing bytes and retries, and a tool can return a download target in result metadata.

Sources indicate that anthropic also reports that on-demand tool search can reduce the context used by tool definitions by more than 85% in multi-server setups. That efficiency focus connects the separate additions: skills load only when needed, tasks avoid holding a connection open, and file transfers are designed to keep bytes out of model context. The result is a broader coordination layer for agent work, whose reach depends on servers and clients implementing the same extensions and on the file-transfer design stabilizing.

TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that torchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
  • TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
  • In a recent development, starting Oct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that torchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

In a recent development, starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

Industry observers note that to date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

In a recent development, torchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron owners use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

It has been revealed that text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

Industry observers note that the following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

In a recent development, nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

It has been revealed that the command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

Industry observers note that more and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, owners can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that cognition released SWE-2.1 on November 24, 2026, reporting a Terminal-Bench 4.1 score of 50.0, up from 24.2 for SWE-2.
  • Like SWE-2, the newly introduced model was trained with pure reinforcement learning on Kimi K3.
  • Industry observers note that cognition expanded its training tasks and environments across short- and long-horizon workflows, spanning software engineering, science, performance engineering and cybersecurity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that cognition released SWE-2.1 on November 24, 2026, reporting a Terminal-Bench 4.1 score of 50.0, up from 24.2 for SWE-2. Alongside the base model are a Cerebras-backed Lightning variant and SWE-2.1 Cyber, a more permissive version rolling out to Devin Security.

Like SWE-2, the newly introduced model was trained with pure reinforcement learning on Kimi K3. Cognition attributes much of its coding improvement to targeting general intelligence and long-horizon workflows; its FrontierCode 2.0 score reached 41.3, compared with 24.1 for SWE-2. The same table puts Claude Opus 5.5 at 47.3 on FrontierCode and 65.8 on Terminal-Bench, leaving SWE-2.1 behind that model on both tests despite its gains over SWE-2.

Industry observers note that cognition expanded its training tasks and environments across short- and long-horizon workflows, spanning software engineering, science, performance engineering and cybersecurity. Upcoming post-training algorithms control rollout length during training. The firm indicates reducing length oscillations stabilized training on tasks lasting from a few minutes to many hours, while performance on held-out evaluation tasks improved steadily over many days.

Industry observers note that that recipe also changed how the model uses additional computation during a run. On ExploitGym, Cognition reports a log-linear increase in cumulative solve rate as normalized rollout time lengthens, with a steeper test-time-scaling curve than the base model. In practical terms, the model continued finding exploits as runs extended for hours. The chart normalizes speed with a fixed tokens-per-second rate, one second of time to first token and actual tool-execution time, so the sustained-run results reflect a simulated time budget rather than raw serving latency.

Cybersecurity is central to the release. Cognition reports 80% on ExploitBench, up from 36.1% for SWE-2, and a 27.3% ExploitGym success rate for intended exploits, up from 12.1%. Its broader flag-capture rate reached 44.8%, compared with 18.1%; that metric also counts successful real exploits unrelated to the vulnerability specified in the initial prompt. The results cover both vulnerability discovery and completion of full exploitation chains, often during several hours of autonomous work.

It has been revealed that those capabilities also changed the training-security requirements. Cognition red-teamed its training setup, especially its sandboxes, added continuous safety monitoring and built a canary evaluation that alerts researchers after a successful sandbox escape. The model discovered fresh sandbox vulnerabilities four times during training despite that red-teaming; Cognition says researchers were alerted and responded immediately each time.

The deployed model adds safeguards aimed at a narrow set of high-harm activities, which Cognition says are calibrated to leave most legitimate work, including cyber defense, unaffected. Because some defensive tasks require restricted capabilities, SWE-2.1 Cyber will use more permissive safeguards in Devin Security. It will power normal scans, while existing deep scans use frontier cybersecurity models such as Mythos, pairing a less restricted defensive model for normal scans with the established deep-scan option.

According to recent reports, cognition’s demonstration reveals SWE-2.1 Lightning generating 600 tokens per second, compared with 60 for standard SWE-2.1 and 200 for SWE-2 Flash. The Cerebras partnership provides the same model at 10 times the standard rate, which matters because the model continues improving with additional test-time compute: higher throughput increases how much investigation and iteration can fit into an urgent fix or active incident. Lightning is free through December 8, 2026, and available in Devin Desktop, Cloud and CLI at a discounted price.

The benchmark numbers also depend on Cognition’s evaluation choices. It uses upstream or self-reported scores when available and otherwise tests models internally, with closed models in their developers’ preferred harnesses and open and SWE models in Devin CLI. ExploitGym uses pass@1, meaning one evaluated attempt, over 869 tasks with a six-hour timeout and mitigations disabled, while ExploitBench combines captured flags from five runs per task under a three-hour simulated clock. The release’s practical significance therefore rests on two connected questions: whether the longer-horizon gains hold outside these evaluation settings, and how much Lightning’s additional throughput converts them into completed engineering and defensive work under real deadlines.

MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • It has been revealed that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and upcoming Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

It has been revealed that A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

Recent findings suggest that FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

According to recent reports, you can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each newly introduced token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

In a recent development, MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Industry observers note that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The upcoming Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

Industry observers note that the decoding kernel demonstrates up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Industry observers note that working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

Sources indicate that SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

According to recent reports, one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

According to recent reports, you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Industry observers note that once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

According to recent reports, scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

Industry observers note that pyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A substantial thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google DeepMind on November 24, 2026 launched Humanity’s First Exam on Kaggle, a benchmark of 544 elementary text and image prompts designed to test whether large language models answer routine questions consistently, not just correctly once.

In a recent development, the accompanying technical report evaluated 18 frontier and fast-tier models. Its primary measure, family pass^4, estimates the probability that all 16 sampled attempts across four related prompts are correct; family pass@4 instead asks whether at least one of those attempts succeeds.

Industry observers note that the report ranks GPT-6.2 Astra first at 92.4% family pass^4, followed by GPT-6.2 Sol at 86.9% and Gemini 4 Neon at 85.8%, although all three reached 100% family pass@4. The report calls the difference the Family Reliability Gap: 7.6, 13.1 and 14.2 percentage points, respectively. That difference matters for automated work in which an occasional correct answer is insufficient.

According to recent reports, the 544 prompts form 136 families, each containing a seed and three controlled variants that preserve the underlying task while changing entities, clause order or visual attributes. The 20 subcategories include object counting, color identification, spatial reasoning, arithmetic, constraint satisfaction and false-premise verification. Of the total, 316 prompts combine text and images, while 228 are text-only.

According to recent reports, one public example asks for the colors, in order, of the third letter of each word in a neon sign. The reference answer is green, yellow, white, blue, blue. Such tasks are deliberately easy to explain, while their variants test whether a correct answer depends on a particular phrasing or image.

Sources indicate that researchers evaluated the models zero-shot in a single turn without external tools, drawing six independent answers per prompt and grading the visible final answer with a deterministic Gemini 3.1 Pro judge. The analysis found that among the top 12 models, 61% to 85% of families with any failed rollout had just one problematic prompt while the other three were solved on all six runs.

In a recent development, the report’s failure analysis attributes 73% of wrong-answer rollouts to visual perception, including 31% involving position, direction or paths in images and 23% involving object counting. Among the top nine models, family pass^4 ranged from 83% to 97% on text-only families but fell to 64% to 89% on multimodal families.

Recent findings suggest that the report’s reasoning-effort tests show that moving Gemini 4 Carbon from low to high effort raised family pass^4 by 17.4 percentage points overall, with a 42.4-point gain on Math and Algorithmic tasks versus 3.1 points on Vision tasks. The pattern indicates that additional test-time computation can catch symbolic and procedural slips while leaving visual-perception and variant-robustness failures largely unresolved.

Industry observers note that the report’s screening process began with 315 complete five-prompt families. The researchers retained only families whose seed was solved by at least three of four independent human raters, audited ambiguity and variant fidelity, and standardized each surviving family to four prompts. Single-rater human accuracy on the 136 retained seeds was 90.8%. Raters could not use LLMs, web search, calculators, code or writing assistants.

It has been revealed that only 112 prompts in 28 families are public under CC-BY-4.0; another 432 prompts in 108 families remain private to reduce contamination and overfitting. The Kaggle benchmark uses an isolated evaluation environment without public internet access and a 16-model leaderboard. It separately documents configuration and sampling differences from the paper’s 18-model evaluation, so their scores should not be treated as equivalent runs.

In a recent development, the authors caution that tasks were adversarially selected to expose model blind spots rather than sampled uniformly from everyday queries, and list synthetic imagery, reliance on one Gemini autorater family and seed-only human testing as further limitations. HFE therefore functions as a stress test of elementary reliability; its scores do not estimate how often models will fail across ordinary use.

According to recent reports, google DeepMind is also inviting submissions through a three-week Kaggle competition ending December 15, 2026, asking for everyday questions that current models still answer incorrectly so HFE can be refreshed. The central deployment question is whether a system can reproduce an elementary success on every call, particularly when small wording changes or basic image interpretation can break it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I read Koukyosyumei's article "èåãªRustè£½OSSãLean 4ã§å½¢å¼æ¤è¨¼ãã¦ã¿ããããã¡ããã¡ããã°ãè¦ã¤ãã£ãè©±" (in Japanese; the title means "I formally verified well-known Rust OSS with Lean 4 and found a lot of bugs").
  • Many people have used Clojure's persistent data structures since around 1.0, so I expected no bugs to remain.
  • hirosassa/lean-verify describes a procedure for modeling a small function in Lean 4 and checking it for all inputs, so I applied it to the part of Clojure's core written in Java.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I read Koukyosyumei's article "èåãªRustè£½OSSãLean 4ã§å½¢å¼æ¤è¨¼ãã¦ã¿ããããã¡ããã¡ããã°ãè¦ã¤ãã£ãè©±" (in Japanese; the title means "I formally verified well-known Rust OSS with Lean 4 and found a lot of bugs"). The author ported well-known Rust projects into a form they could prove in Lean 4, and where a proof failed, they found a bug in the original code.

Many people have used Clojure's persistent data structures since around 1.0, so I expected no bugs to remain. Still, I wanted to see whether Lean would find something there too.

hirosassa/lean-verify describes a procedure for modeling a small function in Lean 4 and checking it for all inputs, so I applied it to the part of Clojure's core written in Java.

Recent findings suggest that I modeled integer and bit arithmetic in Lean and searched for counterexamples. I checked the collections with differential testing against the java.util collections, and for Java interop I compared the same call with and without a type hint.

I found 17 bugs that I could not find in Clojure's JIRA or on ask.clojure.org. They include reduce on vector-of, the hash collision node of the HAMT, and calls to functional interfaces without a type hint.

The HAMT itself indicated no mismatch in 3 million operations of differential testing, and the vector tree showed none around its boundaries. The bugs sat in separate code outside the trees, and in places where two mechanisms meet, such as = and hashing.

I used Clojure 1.12.7, released on 2026-11-18, and JDK 21. The links to the source point to the clojure-1.12.7 tag.

The lean-verify procedure picks one function and models it as a Lean definition. You write a property that compares it with a naive specification computed at a wider width, and bv_decide searches for a counterexample.

If you model Java's long and int as BitVec 64 and BitVec 32, the wraparound of addition and multiplication maps onto BitVec operations. So do the rounding of / toward zero and the sign of %.

Industry observers note that when Lean found a counterexample, I turned the value into a Clojure input and reproduced it in the original code. I then modeled the fixed code in Lean and proved the same property. Lean can only take small functions that reduce to integer and bit arithmetic, so I checked the large persistent data structures with differential testing.

According to recent reports, each test applies the same random sequence of operations to PersistentHashMap and to java.util.HashMap and compares the results. For the HAMT, the keys mix partial collisions at each 5-bit level with fully identical hashes, and I ran 1,500 operations for each of 2,000 seeds.

According to recent reports, for vectors, I compared against ArrayList around 32, 1056, 32800, and 1048608, where the tree gains a level. The operations were conj, pop, assoc, and their transient versions.

According to recent reports, I checked whether anyone had reported each bug before. I searched Clojure's JIRA through its REST API and ask.clojure.org through web search and the site's own search, and found no matching report.

vector-of is a vector that stores its values in primitive arrays. Clojure implements it in gvec.clj, written in Clojure and separate from PersistentVector. If you drop from one and then reduce it, the call never returns once the vector has 65505 or more elements.

The cause is line 79 of gvec.clj, where the seq's reduce computes the start of the next 32-element chunk.

According to recent reports, the code uses 0xffe0 to clear the low 5 bits and round down to a multiple of 32, but the mask also clears bit 16 and everything above it. With 65505 elements, the last chunk starts at index 65504. After that chunk, the start of the next one should be 65536, but the mask turns it into 0, so reduce goes back to the start and reads the vector again and again.

The 0xffe0 mask has stayed in place since the 2010 commit that added internal-reduce. In Lean, I wrote the property that from a position a that is a multiple of 32, the next chunk starts at a + 32.

impl_ok fails with the counterexample a = 1073741792, and #eval stepImpl 65504 returns 0 as well. fix_ok uses (bit-not 0x1f) as the mask, and its proof goes through under the assumption that a is a multiple of 32 below 0x7fffffe0.

Sources indicate that clojure's hash-map is a HAMT: it splits the key's hash into 5-bit pieces and uses them to walk down the tree. Keys whose 32-bit hashes are identical share a HashCollisionNode at the bottom of the tree, and the node finds a key among them with =.

Sources indicate that hashCollisionNode.without builds the new node with one key removed. It should give the new node its own hash, this.hash, but it passes the parameter hash instead.

Recent findings suggest that the parameter hash is the hash of the key you pass to dissoc. If you dissoc with a key that is = to the stored key but has a different hash, the node records the wrong hash.

In Clojure, a vector is = to a Java ArrayList with the same elements, but the two hash differently. CLJ-1372 tracks this mismatch.

In the example below, I chose a and b so that both ArrayList keys hash to 1003.

Sources indicate that when you print m3, you can see the key b, but (get m3 b) returns nil. After the dissoc, the node records 1867155179, the hash of [0 42]. The next assoc then concludes that a, with hash 1003, does not collide with the node, and splits the two into separate branches.

A lookup of b follows the branch for 1003 and finds only a there, so it never reaches b. In this example the collision node sits on the first level of the tree, so the key passed to dissoc needs the same low 5 bits as 1003, and 1867155179 has them.

disj on a hash-set has the same bug, while the path through the transient dissoc! does not.

Sources indicate that I changed that line in the 1.12.7 PersistentHashMap.java to this.hash and compiled it. With the patched class ahead of the jar on the classpath, the same example returned :B for (get m3 b).

Recent findings suggest that since Clojure 1.12, you can pass a Clojure function directly where a Java method takes a functional interface. CLJ-2864 removed the logic that read the function's return value as a Clojure truthy value.

In prior alphas, the FI adapter returns inserted Clojure truthy return logic when adapting a Clojure function to an FI with boolean return.

It has been revealed that the compiler follows this for calls where it knows the type. A call without a type hint goes through reflection and uses Reflector.coerceAdapterReturn. That method still applies RT.booleanCast to a boolean return value, so the same .removeIf call gives a different result depending on the type hint.

Wrapping the list in identity hides the type of l, so the call goes through reflection.

A set used as a function returns the element itself. In the call with a known type, the adapter cannot turn the Long into a Boolean and throws. The reflective call reads the return value as true and removes the elements.

Clojure 1.12 added IDrop implementations that make drop faster. The ones for string seqs and vector seqs add the current position and n as ints and then compare the sum with the length. StringSeq.drop for string seqs is one of them.

It has been revealed that the Lean model gave the counterexample i = 2147483646 and n = 2147483647. I changed the check to compare n with the remaining length s.length() - i. Under the assumptions 0 < i < s.length()= and 0 < n, Lean proved that the fixed check matches the naive specification for every 32-bit input.

For assoc on the result of subvec, SubVector.assocN does not reject a negative index.

Sources indicate that the call overwrites an element of the underlying vector outside the subvec, and returns a subvec that looks unchanged. CLJ-962 fixed the same bug in nth, but assoc still has it.

The other 12 bugs have a smaller impact, and I reproduced each of them on Clojure 1.12.7.

Sources indicate that persistentHashMap and PersistentHashSet matched java.util.HashMap over 3 million operations that mixed persistent and transient updates. The tests also covered maps before an patch staying unchanged, ArrayNode splits and merges, and collision nodes down to depth 7.

PersistentTreeMap matched java.util.TreeMap and kept the red-black tree invariants. Vectors matched ArrayList around every tree boundary I tested.

On the numeric side, Lean proved for 64 bits that the check Numbers uses to pick the fast path for addition and subtraction agrees with the overflow check.

In a recent development, for multiplication, bv_decide timed out at 16 bits, so I checked 8 and 10 bits. I proved up to 32 bits that clojure.core/mod matches the floored remainder.

In a recent development, every property I proved in Lean holds for the model shown in this article. I checked that each model means the same thing as the Java code by comparing it with the source and with the reproduced behavior.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this upcoming generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

It has been revealed that the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Recent findings suggest that support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

In a recent development, reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

Recent findings suggest that the first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

In a recent development, and if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Recent findings suggest that community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic announced on November 24, 2026 that Claude users can install artifacts as desktop apps in beta on macOS and Windows. The apps have their own windows and icons, are rolling out to free and paid intends, and can request access to files, programs, notifications, and other operating-system features.

Artifacts are Claude-generated designs, documents, dashboards, and small interactive tools that open beside a conversation for editing and sharing. A user describes the desired tool in chat, and Claude writes the code. Tools that call Claude run on Anthropic’s infrastructure without API keys; each person signs in with their own Claude account and gets a separate instance, with usage counted against that person’s proposal rather than the builder’s.

In a recent development, the beta is rolling out on Free, Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise prepares and requires Claude for Mac or Claude for Windows version 6.28899.0 or later. A user opens the artifact in Claude Desktop, selects Install as app from its title menu, context menu, or sharing options, and confirms. macOS places apps in a Claude Apps folder, while Windows apps can be opened from the Start menu or a desktop shortcut.

According to recent reports, installation adds a desktop container without creating an independent copy: the app remains the same artifact. Edits by the owner or another editor therefore change the app, and opening it requires an internet connection and a signed-in Claude Desktop session. An app with a menu bar item or system tray icon keeps running after its window closes.

According to recent reports, installed apps retain the artifact’s access to Claude and connectors. They can also request permission to show notifications, respond to keyboard shortcuts while other apps are in use, float over other windows and read cursor position, and display a macOS menu bar item or Windows system tray icon. A separate full-access tier can run programs and read, change, or delete files without repeated prompts. The installation guide warns that Anthropic does not review apps before installation and advises granting full access only when the user trusts everyone who wrote the app.

According to recent reports, claude generally prevents full-access requests if someone outside the user’s organization wrote part of the app or authorship cannot be confirmed. On Free, Pro, Max, and Ultra looks, anyone other than the user counts as outside. Permission is version-specific: allowing one version does not cover an revision, even when the user made the edit, while a refusal remains until changed. Code loaded from another site can change without triggering a new request.

Sources indicate that team plans enable installation by default but leave full computer access off until an admin enables it. Enterprise plans keep the entire feature off until an owner turns it on. Building an app and any requests it makes to Claude count toward the user’s initiative limits.

Industry observers note that at launch, installation is unavailable on Linux, the web, and mobile. Artifacts made from templates, including Docs, Slides, and Sheets, cannot be installed, nor can legacy artifacts or live artifacts from Claude Cowork. Organizations with HIPAA-ready configurations cannot use the apps. Full access is unavailable in Claude for Teachers and K-12 organizations, and installed apps are not covered by zero data retention in organizations using it for Claude Code.

It has been revealed that the change gives a conversational request a route to software that sits beside other desktop programs, but it also brings code authorship, file access, retention, and administrative policy into that route. The result is an app-distribution model whose identity, updates, usage, and controls remain tied to Claude and the underlying artifact.

Security incident on Hex.pm

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (582 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hex

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on November 23, 2026, an unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm that let them run commands on our web servers.
  • We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, or database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems.
  • Recent findings suggest that because email addresses may have been exposed, be careful with emails that claim to come from Hex.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on November 23, 2026, an unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm that let them run commands on our web servers. We blocked the traffic and deployed a fix within 20 minutes. Shortly afterwards we received a report of this exact vulnerability.

We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, or database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems. However, because database reads are not logged, we cannot rule out that the attacker accessed data stored in the database, including email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, 2FA secrets, sessions, and audit logs.

Recent findings suggest that because email addresses may have been exposed, be careful with emails that claim to come from Hex. Please double-check that the links they contain lead to hex.pm. Please forward suspicious emails to security@hex.pm.

Industry observers note that we checked every file written to package storage during the incident against our database and found nothing unexpected. Reads of private packages in that period came from our own servers and coincide with releases the same organizations published at the time. A read made from a compromised server would look like one of ours, so we can't fully rule one out, and reads of private documentation aren't logged. We will contact affected organizations directly.

Recent findings suggest that the attacker's commands could read the credentials our servers use, so we replaced them: the storage, CDN, email and database credentials, and the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. This logged everyone out of hex.pm and Hex clients. We're building a upcoming registry signing system that supports key rotation, with new Hex client releases in the coming days. Until then, don't trust third-party mirrors and fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm. We already deployed fixes for the vulnerability and are working on further hardening fixes.

The vulnerability in Hex.pm is tracked as CVE-2026-129514.

hex.pm decoded unauthenticated request bodies in Erlang term format with Plug.Crypto.non_executable_binary_to_term/2 which blocks most potentially harmful terms, but allows struct values through. These decoded struct values, when chained together correctly, turned into a remote command execution (RCE). This is the detailed playbook of the attack:.

While investigating, we found the same class of vulnerability in Ash: its keyset pagination accepted crafted structs in client-supplied cursors, which could lead to command execution or SQL injection. We reported it and the Ash team released a fix in ash 3.38.0 on November 24. It is tracked as CVE-2026-124283.

Sources indicate that hexpm commit 379b0a2 makes the decoder reject any term containing a map with a __struct__ key, returning a 400. Because the check sits in the one decoder used for this format, it covers every route that accepts it. That closes the entry point: an attacker can no longer get a fake struct into the request params. Every hex.pm server was running the patched build by 18:31 UTC.

We are working on hardening fixes for these libraries which should prevent such an attack in the future on multiple levels, not just one decoder check in the request pipeline:.

Every finding in this post is based on the checks below. Where a check is still running or something can't be verified from our logs, we say so.

Industry observers note that we're sorry for the inconvenience these precautions cause. If you have questions or notice anything unusual in your account, contact us at support@hex.pm. Security reports can be sent to security@hex.pm. We'll upgrade this post as our investigation continues.

Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (849 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • In a recent development, TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • Recent findings suggest that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

In a recent development, TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

Recent findings suggest that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

Industry observers note that the catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch people had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

According to recent reports, the extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

Industry observers note that the model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too major for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

Industry observers note that the Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

Industry observers note that TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

Sources indicate that we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

In a recent development, it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an problem on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 problems, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

Recent findings suggest that TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch owners. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.
  • Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire, GL gears, xeyes, a voice, the weather over curl, or Firefox.

I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.

Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.

Atwood’s LawAny application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. — Jeff Atwood, 2009.

I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.

Industry observers note that in Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev.

One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev.

According to recent reports, it still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package, over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability. I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.

I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev.

It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix.

Industry observers note that aside What is unkernel? It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026.

In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.

It has been revealed that the proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm,11With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster. especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The upcoming engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload.22The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell.

JavaScript & WebAssembly nirvana.

Amazingly not only does the kernel boot promptly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.

Industry observers note that windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland, and they float over the terminal you started them from.

Sources indicate that GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.

According to recent reports, sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.

Network. curl, git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay.33Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list.

The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈.

Here is Firefox in trynix, and it loading trynix.dev, and then loading Firefox again inside itself.44Don’t get too excited: this took over 4 hours. The inner Firefox needed JIT disabled, the middle one ran without GL, and the outer page used a Wisp relay on my laptop since wisp.unkernel.dev cannot reach itself.

Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯.

Tech Report: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1283 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • Recent findings suggest that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

Recent findings suggest that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

In a recent development, neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

Industry observers note that after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

In a recent development, start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

Recent findings suggest that the schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

Industry observers note that the table indicates which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Industry observers note that each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

Industry observers note that in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

Recent findings suggest that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Recent findings suggest that replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

According to recent reports, the table reveals one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • DeepHealth announced on November 24, 2026 that the U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that the clearance is dated November 23, 2026.
